entities.summary:
The African National Congress (ANC) is South Africa's ruling party and one of the world's most historic liberation movements, founded in 1912 as the South African Native National Congress. Leading the struggle against apartheid for 82 years, the ANC brought Nelson Mandela to the presidency in South Africa's first democratic elections in April 1994, ending white minority rule and creating a constitutional democracy.

Founded by John Langalibalele Dube, Pixley ka Isaka Seme, and Sol Plaatje in Bloemfontein, the ANC was initially a moderate organization seeking civil rights within the existing system. The 1948 election of the National Party and the institutionalization of apartheid radicalized the ANC. The 1960 Sharpeville massacre, where police killed 69 peaceful protesters, led to the ANC's banning and the formation of its armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe ('Spear of the Nation'), which Nelson Mandela helped found.

Mandela's imprisonment (1964-1990) transformed him into a global symbol of resistance while the ANC maintained the struggle in exile from Zambia and Tanzania. The 1994 elections — in which Mandela won with 62.6% of the vote — became one of the 20th century's most celebrated moments. The ANC governed South Africa continuously from 1994, but corruption scandals under Jacob Zuma (2009-2018), declining service delivery, and 50% unemployment rates eroded the ANC's majority, which fell below 50% for the first time in the May 2024 elections.
